title: These and these (Eruvin 13b)
hook: both schools speak the words of the living God; the law follows Hillel because his students were humble and cited Shammai first

segments.voice: Yesterday Elijah told how God smiled when the sages won the argument. Your line was my children won.

An argument in a comment thread rarely ends with anyone reading the other side. Each person waits for the other to stop typing, then says their own thing again, louder. The Talmud tells of an argument that went on for three years, between two whole schools of scholars: the students of Hillel and the students of Shammai. Each said: the law follows us. Finally, the Talmud says, a voice came from heaven to settle it. What it said is not what you'd expect.
screen: `NOBODY READS THE OTHER SIDE.` → `THREE YEARS OF ARGUMENT.` → `A VOICE TO SETTLE IT.`

segments.voice: In tractate Eruvin, the heavenly voice says: these and these are the words of the living God. And the law follows the school of Hillel. Both sides are speaking the words of the living God; the argument itself is holy. And yet practical life needs one ruling, so the law goes with Hillel. Then the Talmud asks the obvious question: if both are the words of the living God, why does Hillel's school win? Its answer isn't that they were smarter. It's that they were gentle and humble. They studied their own opinions and the opinions of Shammai's school. And when they taught, they quoted Shammai's view first, before their own. The side that won is the side that stated the other side first, and fairly. The passage ends with a line about humility: whoever makes himself small, the Holy One lifts up; whoever chases greatness, greatness runs away from him. There's a puzzle here. Two days ago the sages refused a voice from heaven. Here they accept one. Later commentators ask why, and one answer some give is that this voice agreed with where the majority already stood. But the bigger lesson is the one in the middle. Shammai's words stay in the Talmud, printed on the page right next to Hillel's. The losing side is kept, honored, and still studied.
screen: `THESE AND THESE: BOTH ARE LIVING WORDS.` · `THE LAW FOLLOWS HILLEL.` · `THEY QUOTED SHAMMAI FIRST.` · `THE LOSING SIDE IS KEPT.` · then, large: `THESE AND THESE.`

segments.voice: Think of a disagreement you're in right now, politics, family, work, anything, and before your own view, say the other person's view silently, in the strongest and fairest words you can: the way they'd say it, not the way you'd mock it. Keep at it until they'd nod and say, yes, that's what I mean, and only then let your own view come back.
Hillel, whose students quoted Shammai's view before their own, and whose school the law followed, because these and these were both the words of the living God.
Your line: quote the other side first. Humility, not cleverness, decided the law. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish study keeps minority and rejected opinions on the page beside the ruling, and eilu v'eilu, these and these, is often quoted to honor respectful disagreement.

fork.setup: you're teaching a ruling your school won. the other school disagreed. how do you teach it?
options: quote their view first, then yours.
teach their view as a mistake to avoid.
fork.reveal: Hillel's school quoted Shammai's view first, and the Talmud says that humility is why the law follows them.

original.note: Hebrew: these and these, from Eruvin 13b.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone's right, so it doesn't matter.
what it means: both sides are holy, a ruling is still needed, and humility decides it.
what a scholar hears: the full phrase is eilu v'eilu divrei Elohim chayyim, and the Talmud's next question is why Hillel's school wins at all.
guess: the sage whose school quoted the other side first
the sage whose school won by sheer brilliance
a strict sage whose rulings were struck from the books

notes: Eruvin 13b paraphrased: the three-year dispute, the bat kol, the reasons (pleasant and humble, studied both views, cited Shammai first), and the humility saying.

The contrast with Bava Metzia 59b (a bat kol refused there, accepted here) is discussed by commentators (e.g. Tosafot on Bava Metzia 59b); the script gives one common answer. Please confirm the attribution.
Mishnah Eduyot lists the few cases where the law follows Beit Shammai; 'with few exceptions' in the trapdoor reflects this.
